newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia bonds recover in unexpected fashion.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia bonds recover in unexpected fashion.

text.p: *Australian bond yields closed sharply lower, wiping out the heavy sell-off seen late last week, as the Reserve Bank suprised everyone in cutting official interest rates to 6.0 percent.

Australian bond yields closed sharply lower, wiping out the heavy sell-off seen late last week, as the Reserve Bank surprised the markets by cutting official interest rates by 50 basis points to 6.0 percent.
Although many analysts had been predicting a further easing, most thought a cut would be on hold until early next year at the earliest after the RBA board left policy unchanged last week.
Three-year bond yields dropped to the lowest level in nearly three-years, but 10-year bond yields, while showing a double digit yield fall, failed to breach the elusive 7.0 percent.

"The failure of the 10-year bond to break below 7.0 percent, despite cash now at 6.0 percent, suggests that the markets want rolled gold evidence that the risk premium on Australia warrants a flatter yield curve," said Stephen Koukoulas, chief economist at Citibank Australia.
The yield curve steepened sharply, with the three/10-year bond yield spread jumping to 87 basis points, its highest level since late September.
The RBA said the rate cut reflected the improved inflation outlook and expects underlying inflation to be under 2.5 percent for the rest of fiscal year 1996/97.
It also expects this good inflation performance to continue into 1997/98.
But economists at Macquarie Bank feel that today's rate cut has a hint of "panic" on the part of the authorities.

"With the authorities prime concern now unemployment, any sign that economic growth is not making inroads into unemployment suggests another cut in rates cannot be ruled out," Macquarie said in a report.
However, this would also point to an even stronger acceleration in growth next year, which will raise concerns about future inflation, it added.
Thursday sees the release of the November labour force report, which is expected to show sluggish employment growth.

Today's flurry of local data was slightly overshadowed by the interest rate move, but notably Westpac's latest monthly consumer confidence index dropped 7.4 points, reversing the sharp jump in November.

"In moving to cut interest rates...the Reserve Bank has clearly responded to the overall weakness in the economy exemplified by today's fall in consumer sentiment and the continuing low inflationary outlook," said Westpac's general manager, economics, Bill Evans.

Local yield spreads to the U.S. and Canada shrank after the rate cut, although the long-end margins were above the day's lows. The market also outpaced the rally in New Zealand debt, which followed the formation of a National/N.Z. First coalition government after two months of negotiation.
